defects.justification: Upload, download and delete endpoints have no authentication at all, so anyone who can reach the service can overwrite (?overwrite=true) or delete every stored file; the README only says to add auth later. I would block exposing it as-is.

Files are written in place: overwrite mode truncates the existing file before copying, so concurrent downloads see a partial file and a failure mid-copy (e.g. disk full) destroys the old file and leaves a truncated one (which also blocks retries with 409). Write to a temp file and os.replace it.

Pillow only raises DecompressionBombError above 2x MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS; images between ~89M and ~179M pixels merely warn and are fully decoded, so a small crafted PNG can make each thumbnail request allocate hundreds of MB.

The temp file name `<size>.tmp` is shared by all concurrent requests for the same thumbnail, so two simultaneous requests write the same temp file and one os.replace can publish a half-written PNG or fail with FileNotFoundError (500).
Only UnidentifiedImageError and DecompressionBombError are caught; a truncated or corrupt image raises OSError during thumbnail()/save(), producing a 500 instead of the documented 415.

`/files/..%2Fsecret` is decoded to a path with a slash that never matches the `/files/<name>` route, so the 404 comes from Flask routing and the test does not exercise the file_path() name validation it claims to cover.
Dependencies use open-ended `>=` ranges (flask, pillow, pytest); Pillow in particular has frequent security releases and breaking changes, so the version should be pinned.
